devices_later.title: Not in this release
devices_later.description:
⚠️ **Sensors and controls are not in this release.** This is an early alpha, and it exists to gather readings.

Setting up the inverter properly — including taking over the entity IDs of the YAML package, which is the one decision here that cannot be undone — comes in a later release.

Pressing **Submit** sets this entry up for **diagnostics only**: it connects to your inverter, works out what it is and which registers it answers, and creates no entities for the values. You can upgrade it to a full entry later without deleting it.

entity_ids.title: Existing entities found
entity_ids.description:
Home Assistant found **{count} entities** from the `modbus_sungrow.yaml` package, such as `{example}`. Your recorder history, your statistics and every dashboard card are stored against those entity IDs.

{status}

**Migrate my existing entities** takes those IDs over. History and statistics carry on uninterrupted and your dashboards keep working unchanged. Nothing is copied and nothing is deleted.

**Start fresh** gives this inverter its own IDs, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_dc_power`. Your old history stays where it is, under the old IDs, and your dashboards keep pointing at it.

Either way the entities are identical in every other respect.

find.title: Where is the inverter?
find.description: Searching is usually easier: many people cannot say what their inverter's IP address is without going to look at the router. The search only probes addresses on the range you confirm.

manual.title: The inverter's address
manual.description:
The inverter's IP address, and the Modbus TCP port and device address it answers on. The defaults are right for almost every installation: port 502, device address 1.

If the inverter is behind a WiNet-S dongle, this is the dongle's address rather than the inverter's own. Give the address a reservation in your router first -- an inverter that moves has to be set up again.{error}

data_description.port: 502 unless somebody changed it. A Sungrow Logger uses 503.
data_description.unit_id: 1 for a single inverter. A second inverter in a master/slave cluster answers on 2, and its own address is the one to give here.

name.title: What should this inverter be called?
name.description:
You have **{count}** inverters, and both would otherwise be called “{model}” — Home Assistant would add `_2` to whichever you set up second, which records the order you clicked in and nothing else.

This name becomes part of every entity id for this inverter, for example `{example}`. That is what your history and dashboards are keyed to, so it is worth a moment now: renaming later changes the label but leaves the ids already created exactly where they are.

Something about where it is works best — `Roof`, `Garage`, `Barn`. The suggestion is the most the inverter itself can tell us.

data_description.name: Suggested: {suggestion}. Change it to whatever you will recognise.

nothing_found.title: No inverter found

other_inverter.title: What is the other inverter?
other_inverter.description:
The make, and its size if you know it — *Fronius Symo 8.2*, or *5 kW string inverter on the south roof*. The size is the useful part: it says how large the gap in the load figures is.

This goes into the document, so leave out serial numbers, addresses and names. You can leave it blank.

pick.title: Inverters found
pick.description:
{count} device(s) answered and identified themselves. Names come from your router's DNS where it provides them, otherwise the address is shown.

If none of these is the inverter you meant, choose the last option and you can enter its address yourself.{note}

testimony.title: What do you want to tell us?
testimony.description:
You chose diagnostics only, which means this entry exists to produce a reading — so these are the questions that reading needs and no register can answer.

{measured}

Everything here is optional, and leaving a field empty is honest: it records that the question was not answered, which is different from answering "I don't know". You can change any of it later under the integration's options.

Afterwards, press **Run capability survey** on the device page.

data_description.reporter: Credited in the published reading, and who gets asked if a row raises a question. Leave empty to contribute anonymously.
data_description.survey_transport: Cable against dongle is measured already. What only you know is whether a dongle is on its Ethernet socket or its WiFi — a WiNet-S answers identically either way, so "not sure" is a real answer and better than a guess.
data_description.survey_proxy: modbus-proxy, evcc's proxy, a Home Assistant add-on. A proxy holds one connection and lends it out, so it changes what a dropped register means — and it rebuilds every frame, which can hide or create the frame quirks this project tracks.
data_description.survey_pollers: This Home Assistant is recorded automatically. What matters here is anything else: another Home Assistant, the YAML package, evcc, a logger. An inverter grants very few connections, and two clients competing for one looks exactly like a broken register.
data_description.survey_other_inverter: Your Sungrow does not measure how much your house is using — it works it out from its own output plus what the grid meter says is coming in. A second inverter feeding the same meter therefore makes every load figure too low, by exactly what that inverter is producing, while everything else reads normally. No register can tell us: the Sungrow cannot see it. Say yes and we will ask what it is.
data_description.survey_battery: No register reports it. "SBR096" or "Pylontech Force H1, 14.4 kWh" is more useful than a capacity the inverter already reports.
data_description.survey_comment: Anything unusual about the installation — a cluster, a second inverter, a wallbox, a firmware update you remember.
data_description.publish_address: On, and yours to turn off before you submit. Only the last two octets ever reach the document — never the third, which is what would identify your network — and clear this and it reads xxx.xxx instead. What it buys is telling several readings from one house apart: a master, a slave and two dongles otherwise produce four files that look alike.
data_description.survey_register_dump: On, and worth turning off if you are in a hurry. Without it a survey reads the registers this integration already knows about and takes a couple of seconds. With it, it also sweeps 1510 addresses across twelve bands, including the ones no specification documents — which is how every undocumented register this project knows was found. That is slow because an address with nothing behind it goes quiet rather than refusing, so each empty one costs a full timeout: about five minutes on a direct cable, and considerably longer through a WiNet-S or a VPN. Your inverter keeps being polled throughout, and the survey button on the device page shows how far along it is.

user.title: What is this for?
user.description:
**Set up my inverter** is what you want if you came here to see your solar production in Home Assistant.

**Diagnostics only** connects to the inverter, works out what it is and what it answers, and creates **no entities at all**. It exists because this project has to *measure* which registers each model and firmware supports — Sungrow's own specification has been wrong in both directions — and today that evidence comes from four houses.{mode_choice}

menu_options.setup_devices: Set up my inverter — sensors, controls, the lot
menu_options.setup_diagnostics: Diagnostics only — help this project, create no entities

create_entry.diagnostics:
**You are set up, and nothing has been read yet.** Two more steps, both on the device page this dialog is about to show you:

1. Press **Run capability survey**, under *Diagnostic*. It reads and never writes. On a cable it is over in a couple of minutes with the register sweep on; over a VPN it can take considerably longer, and the three sensors beside the button say how far along it is and what it is reading.
2. When it finishes, open **Notifications** in the sidebar — the badge at the bottom left. The notification there carries a summary and a **Download the document** link. That link is the JSON file to send us, and it stops working after an hour.

Missed it, or came back the next day? **Download diagnostics** on the same device page carries the same document and never expires. Send either to the issue tracker or to Discord.

The file names your inverter by a stand-in rather than its serial number, and carries the last two octets of its address only while that box is ticked.

preview_release.title: Sungrow Modbus is a preview
preview_release.description:
This integration is a preview release, for testers rather than for a system you depend on.

**Entity names may still change.** A name supplies an entity id when the entity is first created, so a change does not move the ids you already have -- your history and dashboards are safe. What it does mean is that your ids can end up differing from somebody who installs later. Where that matters, a rename will ship with a migration that moves yours across and carries the history with it.

**What is not in flux:** readings, units, and the migration from the YAML package. If you chose to keep the YAML package's entity ids, those are reproduced exactly and none of this touches them.

Please report anything that looks wrong -- that is what a preview is for.

control_test_unfinished.description:
The control write test changes a setting, checks it, and changes it back. This one did not get to the changing-back part — Home Assistant was restarted, the entry was reloaded, or the inverter stopped answering partway through.

These settings may still be holding the test's values rather than yours:

{registers}

Fixing this writes each of them back and reads it again to check it took.

init.title: Sungrow Modbus options
init.description:
Everything this integration lets you change, in one place. Open a section to see it; what you do not open stays as it is.

Connection details are not here — changing the host or the unit id means talking to a different device, which is **Reconfigure** rather than an option.

data_description.add_devices: This entry was set up for diagnostics only, so it has no entities. Ticking this asks the one question that was skipped — whether to take over the YAML package's entity ids — and then creates them.{devices_mode}

polling.name: Polling
polling.description:
Registers are read in four groups. Each group is one request cycle, so the interval you set is how often that whole group is fetched.

{tiers}

**Why this is worth changing.** A Sungrow inverter accepts very few Modbus connections at once. If something else polls it — the YAML package, another Home Assistant, EVCC, a logger — you are competing for one, and most reported dropouts are exactly that. Slowing a group down, or switching it off, is the cheapest fix there is.

Set **0** for never: that group is not read at all and its entities are not created. The minimum otherwise is 5 seconds — Sungrow's protocol warns against polling frequently through a WiNet-S dongle, and 5 seconds is already the fastest the YAML package ever used.

Changing anything here reloads the integration.

data_description.realtime: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.
data_description.fast: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.
data_description.medium: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.
data_description.slowest: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.

permissions.name: Permissions
permissions.description:
**Starting and stopping the inverter** is an action rather than a switch, so this integration decides who may call it, and you decide here. Administrators only is the default: there is no way back from a stopped inverter except another call, and the house runs on the grid until somebody makes it.

Opening it to users means users who can already change this device — a read-only login still cannot, and neither setting affects automations or scripts, which act for the household rather than for a person.

**Everything else is not ours to decide, and it is worth knowing what already applies.** The settings this integration exposes — the state-of-charge limits, the EMS mode, the export and power limits — are entities, and Home Assistant checks who may control an entity itself, before any integration is asked. By default a normal user can change all of them and a read-only user none of them. To restrict one person, make their account read-only under *Settings → People*; there is no per-setting permission in Home Assistant for us to offer.

data_description.start_stop: Who may call the start and stop actions on this inverter.
data_description.control_test: Administrators only by default. The control write test changes settings on the inverter and puts them back, and — where you have allowed it above — stops and restarts it. Opening it to users means users who can already change this device; a read-only login still cannot.

external.name: Another inverter on the same supply
external.description:
This inverter works out your house load from its own production and its grid meter. A second, non-Sungrow inverter is invisible to it, so the load reading comes out **low by exactly what that inverter is making** — and negative once it makes more than the house uses.

{reported_load}

Name the entities that report the other inverter's power and this integration adds two corrected sensors. For **energy** in kWh, do not use this page: the Energy dashboard already accepts several solar sources, and adding yours there is both easier and more accurate.

One thing to check when picking a source: some integrations report `unavailable` overnight rather than 0 W. The corrected sensors then go unknown overnight too, because a generator that is not reporting is not the same as one making nothing — assuming zero would put back the very error this page removes.

data.external_sources: Power sensors for the other generation

data_description.external_sources: Only power sensors are listed. Pick every one that reports generation this Sungrow cannot see; leave empty to switch the correction off.
data_description.external_placement: This changes the arithmetic, so it is asked rather than guessed.

advanced.name: Battery and diagnostics
advanced.description:
**Battery charge power.** {battery_status}

The maximum a battery will take is not something the inverter knows — it reports its own converter rating, but not the pack's limit. Sungrow's own technical training recommends the **rated current × the low end of the voltage range**, not the nominal voltage: being conservative here is good for the battery's health.

*Example — a Pylontech Force H1, 14.4 kWh: the datasheet gives a recommended charge current and an operating voltage range per module. Take the current × the lowest voltage in the range, not the nominal one. For a stack reporting 25 A at 355 V that is 25 × 355 ≈ 8875 W, and rounding down to 8500 W costs almost nothing.* Check your own datasheet — the arithmetic is the point, not these numbers.

Leave it at 0 to let the integration work it out.

---

**Diagnostics.** Settings → Devices & Services → Sungrow Modbus → **Download diagnostics** produces a file describing this setup: the model, which capabilities the inverter confirmed, which registers reported themselves unavailable, how each poll group is doing, and why any entity was not created. The serial number and host address are removed from it.

data.register_dump: Include a raw register dump in diagnostics

data_description.battery_max_power: 0 means work it out: a Sungrow pack is identified from the capacity it reports and looked up against its datasheet, and any other pack that reports a BMS charge current gets that instead. Set a value to override either.
data_description.register_dump: Adds every mapped register's raw value. Only useful when a value looks wrong and the decoding itself is in question. Producing it is a second full read of the register map on top of normal polling, which is slow over a WiNet-S dongle, so leave it off unless you have been asked for it.

survey.name: Contribute a capability survey
survey.description:
Sungrow publishes no release notes, and its register specification has been wrong in both directions — so which registers your inverter answers is **measured** rather than looked up. Today that evidence comes from nine readings at four houses, all of them the maintainer's or a friend's, which is why some inverters are supported better than others.

{measured}

Everything below is optional and answers something **no register can**. Leaving a field empty is honest — it records that the question was not answered, which is different from answering "I don't know".

Saving this page keeps your answers. To **run** the survey, press **Run capability survey** on the device page — it shows how far along it is and what it is reading, and offers the finished document as a download when it is done. It reads and never writes, and the serial number is replaced by a stand-in before anything reaches the file.

control_test.name: What the control write test may do
control_test.description:
The **Run control write test** button on the device page does something no other part of this integration does on its own: it **writes** to each setting it can, reads the register straight back, compares what came back against what Sungrow's specification says should be there, and puts your value back.

It exists because a whole class of bug is otherwise invisible. The registers mix units — one battery power setting counts in watts and the one beside it in hundredths of a kilowatt — so a value can be written, read back looking perfectly correct, and still be ten times what you asked for. Reading alone cannot find that. Writing and checking the raw register can.

Everything it changes is changed back and read back before it reports success, and if anything could not be put back you get a repair here telling you exactly what and offering to fix it. The two settings below are the parts that go further than that, and both are off unless you say otherwise.

data.control_test_restart: May it stop and restart the inverter?
data.control_test_export_limit: May it switch feed-in limitation on?

data_description.control_test_restart:
Off by default. With this on, the test writes the stop register, waits for the inverter to report itself stopped, starts it again and times all three transitions — numbers nobody has measured for this hardware, which is why it is worth offering at all.

While it is stopped you generate nothing, the battery neither charges nor discharges, and anything on a backup circuit loses power. Expect tens of seconds; it may be minutes. The inverter is never left stopped: the start is retried on fresh connections, it is started again if Home Assistant shuts down mid-test, and if all of that fails you get a repair that starts it.
data_description.control_test_export_limit:
Off by default. Where you already limit feed-in, the test uses that and this changes nothing. With this on it may also switch the limit on for about a minute where you do not.

Left off because it is the one setting whose failed restore costs you something ongoing rather than just accuracy: an export limit that did not get switched back means you feed in less than you could until somebody notices.

run_control_test.name: Run control write test
run_control_test.description: Writes to every control this integration can write to, checks each one three ways and puts it back. Unlike the capability survey, this CHANGES SETTINGS on the inverter: it limits the battery and the export, and it briefly forces a charge and a discharge. Everything is recorded before the first write and restored afterwards, and the run reports anything it could not put back. It exists because a wrong scale is invisible to a readback -- write 700 W, get 700 W back -- and only writing can find it. The restart and export-limit permissions are set in the integration's options and are off by default.

device_id.description: The Sungrow device to write to, and put back.

run_survey.name: Run capability survey
run_survey.description: Reads this installation's registers and produces a document describing what answered, so support for it can be measured rather than guessed. Reads only; nothing is written to the inverter, and the serial number is replaced by a stand-in. The finished document arrives as a notification with a download link.

start_inverter.name: Start inverter
start_inverter.description: Boots an inverter that has been shut down. Deliberately an action rather than a button: Home Assistant has no confirmation dialog for a button press, and admin rights are required to call this.

stop_inverter.name: Stop inverter
stop_inverter.description: Shuts the inverter down. It stops generating, stops charging and stops discharging until it is started again. Deliberately an action rather than a button, and admin rights are required to call it — a dashboard card cannot do this by accident.
